THE FRUIT OF SIN

Oh no, she had not had an easy time of it during these months she had been at Husaby. She had talked a little with Erlend in the evening, on the day they had been to Medalby. Then she understood that he had thought she was angry with him because he had brought this upon her.

“I remember well enough,” he said very softly. “That day in the spring when we walked in the woods north of the church. I remember well enough that you begged me to leave you be—”

Kristin had been glad because he said this. At other times she often wondered how many things Erlend seemed to have forgotten. But then he said:

“And yet I would not have believed this of you, Kristin—that you could go on like this, nursing a secret grudge against me, while behaving just as sweetly and happily as ever. For you must have known for a long time what was happening to you. I had believed you were as open and honest as the shining sun—”

“Ah, Erlend,” she said sorrowfully. “You of all people in the world know best that I have gone by secret ways and been false to those who trusted me most.” But she wanted so much for him to understand. “And now I do not know whether you remember, my friend, that before this you acted toward me in a way that some would not call honorable. And God and the Virgin Mary know that I bore no grudge, and I loved you no less—”

Erlend’s face softened.

“That was how I thought of it,” he said quietly. “But you know this too—I strove through all these years to make right what I had broken. I comforted myself with the thought that in the end it would come to pass that I could reward you for being so faithful and patient.”

Then she had asked him:

“You have surely heard of my grandfather’s brother and Lady Bengta, who fled from Sweden against the will of her kinsmen. God chastised them by giving them no child together. Have you never feared during all these years that He might punish us in the same way—”

Trembling and softly, she had said to him:

“You can surely understand, my Erlend, that I was not very happy here this summer when this was the first thing that happened to me. And yet I thought— I thought that if you were to die and leave me before we were married, I would rather be left with your child than be alone. I thought that if I were to die bearing it, that would still be better than for you not to have a lawful son who could take your place in the high seat when you must depart from this world—”

Erlend answered vehemently:

“Then I would think my son had been bought far too dearly if he were to cost your life. Do not speak so, Kristin— I do not hold Husaby so dear,” he said a little later. “Especially since I came to understand that Orm can never inherit the ancestral estate after me—”

“Do you care more for her son than for mine?” Kristin asked then.

“Your son—” Erlend laughed a little. “Of him I know no more at present than that he will come here half a year or so earlier than is good. Orm I have loved for twelve years—”

After a while Kristin asked:

“Do you ever long for those children of yours?”

“Yes,” the man answered. “In former times I often went inland to see them in Østerdalen, where they are.”

“You could travel there now during Advent,” Kristin said softly.

“Would you not resent it, then?” Erlend asked happily.

Kristin had answered that she would find it reasonable. Then he had asked whether she would object if he brought the children home with him for Christmas. “At some time you must see them.” And again she had answered that this too seemed reasonable to her.
